storm.summary_layperson: No storms are on radar or headed toward the cove tonight — just a slight chance of an isolated shower or thunderstorm, same as everywhere else nearby.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No storm is currently in play for the Sound's marine layer to blunt or not; for reference, today's 8.3°F air-water gap is projected to fade below the ~5°F protective threshold by about 7:04 PM as the air cools after sunset.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows no cells anywhere near the cove, and there are no NWS watches, warnings, or advisories active. CAPE is a modest 330 J/kg with strong 0-6km bulk shear aloft (45 kt from the west), but with instability this low there's essentially nothing for that shear to organize. The OKX area forecast discussion mentions a west-to-east shower/thunderstorm window developing during and after peak heating this afternoon and evening, with severe chances called "less certain" — that's a general regional mention, not a tracked cell. A separate AFD note about a frontal system with heavier rain applies to Sunday, three days out.

The Sound's usual protective marine layer isn't a factor either way tonight since there's nothing on radar for it to blunt. For reference: water is 74.1°F against 82.4°F air right now, an 8.3°F gap, but that's a moving target — air cools after sunset (7:55 PM) while the Sound stays flat, so the gap is projected to fall under the ~5°F protective threshold around 7:04 PM, and keep sliding negative overnight. A storm that tried to organize earlier in the evening would find a real buffer; one developing after 7 PM would find little to none.

Net effect: the cove and surrounding towns face the same low, mostly cosmetic risk tonight — a stray shower is more likely than an organized thunderstorm, and there's no local mechanism currently amplifying or mitigating anything because nothing is approaching.

Bottom line: nothing to act on. Worth a radar recheck if anything fires up later this evening, particularly after the marine-layer gap collapses near 7 PM, since that's when the cove loses its usual edge over inland spots.

wind.tactics_blurb: RYC is reading a steady NW 11 kt gusting 15 right now — a gradient-wind evening, not a sea breeze (the classic S-SSW thermal axis never shows up in today's obs despite a healthy 8.3°F air-water gap). wind.tactics_detail_html:
This reads as a gradient-wind evening, not a sea-breeze day, even though the air-water temperature difference (deltaT) is a strong 8.3°F — normally plenty to seed a thermal. The two-ingredient sea-breeze test needs deltaT above 5°F and the breeze actually filling in from the classic S-SSW direction for this stretch of coast; only 15% of coastal stations are reading southerly, and the wind at the cove and across the western Sound is blowing from the NW instead. The automated pipeline's deltaT-and-time-of-day proxy flagged today as a sea-breeze day and applied a directional maturation correction, but that correction is built for the S-family sea-breeze axis — with the actual wind sitting in the NW/offshore quadrant, that flag looks like a false positive today, so the call here is gradient-only (B-moderate), not thermal.

What you'll actually feel is a moderate NW-to-WNW breeze, 7-11 kt depending on where you are. RYC (ground truth for the cove) is reading a steady 11.1 kt gusting 15.3, notably stronger than the wider regional gradient (7.6 kt on the authoritative ensemble measure) — a real cove-specific acceleration, likely local channeling as NW flow funnels over Greenwich Point and down through the cove mouth rather than a shelter effect. Per the cove's geography, N-NW flow arrives offshore over land, gusty and puffy with big oscillations (15-30°); the best average pressure sits down the middle of the cove, away from the immediate lee of the NW shore where you'll find the biggest puffs and the deepest holes between them.

Shift character is oscillating but terrain-driven rather than thermal — NW flow over this geography is inherently puffy and shifty, so play the swings rather than committing hard to one side. Because this is a gradient wind, it doesn't care about the sun: it should hold through and past sunset (7:55 PM), likely easing by a knot or two overnight as the boundary layer stabilizes after dark, not collapsing the way a pure sea breeze would.

Worth flagging: HRRR's raw hourly forecast for this window is running well below what's actually on the water — the model shows only 3-6 kt through the evening with direction wandering WNW-NW (295-307°), versus RYC's live 11 kt sustained with gusts to 15 and a firmer NW 310° reading already ahead of where the model expects the evening to end up. Direction agreement across the regional ensemble is a soft 0.61. Given that gap, the table above leans on RYC's live reading and the B-moderate framework (holds through sunset, gentle overnight easing) rather than the model's much lighter numbers.

data_caveats: Buoy 44040 wind/air observation is about 81 min old and the WLIS SST reading is about 93 min old — treat offshore sea-breeze depth and marine-layer numbers as based on slightly stale data.
